TF211497.headline: Same $3.42, a third of the weight
overview: The TF211497 is the second generation of the desert fire-breathing water gun, a compact pistol form with a drum reservoir hanging under the grip and transparent casings on both colourways, one blue and one smoke grey. CASE EJECTION is printed along the flank and the muzzle carries the LED flame effect that gives the fire-breathing family its name. The pack contents are the part that matters commercially: the photographs show two interchangeable battery packs and two USB charging leads, so the unit runs on one cell while the other charges, which is what keeps a water fight going rather than stopping it for a recharge.

This is the lightest and densest model in the whole catalogue. A carton holds 72 pieces at 0.157 CBM and 20.4 kg gross, which works out at 0.28 kg per unit, and a 20GP takes 178 cartons, 12,816 pieces. The 216-piece minimum is three cartons, 0.471 CBM. Because the unit is light and the carton is dense, this is one of the few models here that prices acceptably by air: 216 pieces is 61 kg gross, which is a small air consignment rather than a pallet.

At $3.42 it carries the same unit price as the TF210969 and the TF212706, so the choice between the three is about form rather than cost. The TF210969 is the third-generation volume model at a 240-piece minimum, the TF212706 is the long Ice Burst blaster, and this one is the compact pistol with the spare-cell pack. A buyer who needs the lowest freight per unit and a small entry order will find this the easiest of the three to test, and the two-cell pack is the detail that sells it on the shelf.
visible_features: Pistol form with a drum reservoir mounted under the grip
Transparent casing, supplied in blue and in smoke grey
CASE EJECTION printed along the flank
LED flame effect at the muzzle
Two interchangeable battery packs and two USB charging leads in the pack
72 pieces per carton, 0.28 kg per unit gross

TF212706.headline: The long blaster of the Ice Burst line
overview: The TF212706 is the single-gun version of the Ice Burst design, moulded entirely in transparent blue so the internal mechanism shows through the body. The receiver carries ICE BURST along the flank, the cylindrical module on the top rail is marked Icy Blaze, and the whole upper line is moulded with a rail and a rear serrated section rather than left smooth. The drum reservoir hangs under the grip and the muzzle carries the LED flame effect. It is a longer, flatter silhouette than the pistol-form water guns in this range, which is what makes it read as a blaster on a shelf rather than as a toy handgun.

The carton is a sensible middle. A carton holds 48 pieces at 0.205 CBM and 17.5 kg gross, 0.36 kg per unit, and a 20GP takes 136 cartons, 6,528 pieces. The 144-piece minimum is three cartons and 0.615 CBM, so the entry order is small and the top-up unit is the same carton. Compared with the pair pack TF212709, which ships nine sets per carton at 1.25 kg, this is the cheaper way to put the Ice Burst look on a shelf: one unit, one carton, half the cube per gun.

The three-way choice at this price is worth setting out, because all three sit within four cents of each other. The TF212706 is the long Ice Burst blaster at $3.42 and a 144-piece minimum; the TF211497 is the compact pistol at the same price with two battery cells in the pack; the TF210969 is the third-generation model at the same price with a 240-piece minimum. The Ice Burst is the one to take if the display depends on the look, since the transparent full-length body and the Icy Blaze module are the most distinctive shape of the three.
visible_features: Full transparent blue casing, with the mechanism visible through the body
ICE BURST moulded along the receiver flank
Cylindrical Icy Blaze module mounted on the top rail
Drum reservoir under the grip
Accessory rail along the top line and a serrated rear section
LED flame effect at the muzzle, 0.36 kg per unit gross

TF210951.headline: The reservoir is the ring
overview: The TF210951 makes the water tank the shape of the product. Behind the grip sits a large open ring, moulded in transparent blue, and that ring is the reservoir rather than a decorative frame, so the water level is visible from the side while the gun is in use. The body above it carries SHARK and WATER GUN markings and CASE EJECTION on the rear flank, an accessory rail runs along the top, and the muzzle carries the LED flame effect. It is the most sculptural of the pistol forms here, and the ring is the reason: a customer picks it up because the silhouette is unusual, not because the specification is different.

Logistics are straightforward. A carton holds 36 pieces at 0.152 CBM and 13.5 kg gross, 0.38 kg per unit, and a 20GP takes 184 cartons, 6,624 pieces. The 180-piece minimum is five cartons and 0.76 CBM. The carton weight is low enough that the model can go mixed with lighter items in the same container without upsetting the loading plan, which matters when a buyer is filling a container with several water gun models rather than one.

At $5.31 it sits in the middle of the water gun range, below the TF210956 drum version at $5.46 and above the three $3.42 entry models. The comparison a buyer usually makes is with the TF210956, which takes the same Space body and hangs a drum under it instead of a ring: same family, same design language, $0.15 apart. Taking both is normal, because the ring and the drum photograph as two different products even though they share a body.

TF210956.headline: The Space body with a drum instead of a ring
overview: The TF210956 is the drum version of the Space water gun. It keeps the body of the TF210951, with SHARK and WATER GUN on the flank and CASE EJECTION at the rear, and replaces the ring reservoir with a round drum hung under the grip. Two colourways are produced, transparent blue and transparent smoke, both of which show the water level through the casing. The drum sits lower and further back than the ring does, which changes how the unit balances in the hand: it is the version that reads as a conventional blaster rather than as a design piece.

The packing is better than the ring version's by a clear margin. A carton holds 48 pieces at 0.142 CBM and 15.5 kg gross, only 0.32 kg per unit, and a 20GP takes 197 cartons, 9,456 pieces, against 6,624 for the TF210951. The 144-piece minimum is three cartons and 0.426 CBM. If the order is being planned on freight per unit rather than on how the product looks, this is the more efficient of the two Space models, and the gap is large enough to show in a landed cost.

At $5.46 it is fifteen cents above the ring version and the same distance below the TF210960 at $6.13, so the Space family occupies a tight band in the middle of the range. The practical way to use it is as the volume member of that band: the drum version ships more pieces per container and takes a smaller minimum, so a buyer who wants the Space look as the main line rather than as the accent takes this one and adds the ring version for the display.

TF210960.headline: An optic, a drum and a foregrip
overview: The TF210960 takes the fire-breathing family into a submachine-gun form. The body is longer than the pistol models, with a vertical foregrip under the barrel, a skeleton stock at the rear and a red-dot style optic mounted on the top rail, and the reservoir is a drum under the body rather than under the grip. Two colourways are shown, blue with a clear upper and green with a clear upper, so the coloured lower receiver is the variant rather than the whole body. The muzzle carries the LED flame effect and the flank is printed WATER GUN and CASE EJECTION.

Its carton is one of the most efficient in the range: 18 pieces at 0.087 CBM and 9 kg gross, 0.50 kg per unit, and a 20GP takes 321 cartons, 5,778 pieces. The 144-piece minimum is exactly eight cartons, 0.696 CBM, which is the highest carton count at the minimum anywhere in the water gun range: every other model here starts at three to five cartons. That makes it the one model where the entry order is worth planning against a small LCL shipment rather than a courier.

At $6.13 it is priced against the TF210965 rifle at $10.15 above it and the two Space models below it. The reason to take this rather than a pistol is the optic and the foregrip: the two-handed hold and the sight change how the product is played with, and that is what a parent is buying when they move up from a $3.42 pistol. The green variant also gives a buyer a second colourway inside the same SKU, which is unusual at this price and useful for a display that would otherwise be all blue.

TF210965.headline: The rifle: scope, bipod, box magazine
overview: The TF210965 is the only marksman rifle in the range. It has a long barrel with a suppressor-style tip, a telescopic scope on a raised mount, a folding bipod under the forend, a box magazine and an adjustable stock, and the whole body is moulded in solid blue rather than the transparent casings used lower down the range. The play pattern follows the form: the bipod lets it stand on a surface and the scope gives the child something to sight through, which is why the product photographs show it being fired prone rather than held at the hip.

The pack size reflects the length. Retail packing is 41 x 18.5 x 7 cm, the longest box in this collection, and a carton holds 24 pieces at 0.135 CBM and 14.5 kg gross, 0.60 kg per unit. A 20GP takes 207 cartons, 4,968 pieces, and the 120-piece minimum is five cartons at 0.675 CBM. Because the retail box is long and thin, shelf planning matters more than cube here: this is the model that needs depth on a shelf, so it is usually merchandised standing rather than stacked.

At $10.15 it is the second most expensive water gun after the TF211527 at $14.50, and it earns that on the accessory count rather than on size alone. It is the natural upgrade for a child who already owns one of the pistols, and it gives a retailer a step-up price point between the $7 range and the $14.50 Gatling. For a buyer testing one premium water gun, the choice between this and the Gatling usually comes down to shelf depth: the Gatling is a shorter, taller package.
